comments.author: @claysettlement9757
comments.text:
15:19 - yes, because it is just hype; even the ARC-AGI test results. This entire video is a reading off of Sam Altman's blog, which is a marketing piece. Every time a tech company labels their product as "AI", it is a marketing push. They will use any science fiction comparison possible to sell their stocks, products and services, because when a product looks like fiction on the surface (Benchmarks, Youtube videos, etc) it grabs consumer's attention. They're making a big push towards labelling their latest products as "AGI" or "approaching singularity" because their competition is catching up and they need to push the needle to differentiate themselves. Whether the products actually live up to the hype and can do what they claim (or whether what they claim is actually useful in practical terms) is a completely different story.

The hype in Youtube's Tech Sector is beginning to approach religous cult-level. AGI is a science fiction concept that seems plausible on-paper, but as time goes on it is seeming increasingly impossible, because every time the term is used outside of a fictional setting or philosophical debate, it is being exploited by a business trying to sell a product or gain investors. Tech Influencers are further exploiting this hype to gain views and generate their own income. It is one big cycle.

Who's to say one product is AGI or ASI or whether we've achieve the singularity? I'd argue is isn't the tech company who's so stuck in their insular bubble that they'd have to believe it, or the tech influencers who exploit that hype by jumping on the band-wagon. By those parameters, any discussion of AI, AGI, ASI, or the Singularity are mute, because the parties involved have ulterior moves. This should really be an academic debate, not a discussion between businesses for their customers/followers.

At the end of the day, you need to question "what does the product/service actually do, and how good is it?". Because the discussion online seems to be that, once AGI and then ASI have been invented, we have more or less invented magic, and now the machine will improve itself forever, and it's the last invention we'll ever make, etc. In practical terms, I've used ChatGPT since it launched in December 2022, and while there have been improvements, it hasn't really that changed much. They've added features, but the core performance for most tasks isn't that different (maybe besides it being a bit better at coding).

There's so much hype around what they're promising, but I won't believe it until I actually see results and solutions to problems that work in the long term. Whenever a new feature is announced there's this cycle of "OMG! You can now use ChatGPT advanced voice for language learning!", or "OMG! Now I can generate concept art really quickly!" and then it seems great when you initially use it ... until you use it some more and realise it isn't fit for purpose, and end up going back to traditional methods.

Yes, Advanced Voice can dynamically switch languages, but it also forgets instructions after a few responses and it doesn't have data gained from life experience to relate its lessons back to you, making it more practical to just take a language learning class. Yes, it can generate artwork really quickly, but what it generates is a random guess, which isn't even close to as precise as just hiring an artist or learning those skills yourself; you can make the guesses less random by learning something like Flux with CompifyUI, but that is a whole different pipeline that doesn't fit traditional workplaces. Currently most consumer-level AI products are proof of concepts that kind of work sometimes, but having a machine perform these tasks isn't very intuitive, reliable or practical in the long term when we already have human solutions.

You could say it's OpenAI's goal to market their product as finally achieving AGI so they can raise money and improve their existing features, but that's literally what every business ever wants to do when they use any marketing strategy. They want you to buy into the idea it's "the worst it'll ever be" so you'll give them money now, even though the product isn't there yet.

Lastly: machines can only learn from a data set. We don't have enough data collected anywhere to cover every aspect of the real world. This makes creating a general intelligence impractical, because tech companies are really just taking the data, remixing it, and then applying an algorithm to it to make it perform certain tasks. So like every tech company since the 1950s, they are trying to create a smart machine using code, which as always, isn't going to work. To create a true AI, you would need to give it real world experience by letting it live in the real world and have experiences; so you could say, animals were the real AI all along.

Now that OpenAI is a private company, I think we should all be wary of these kinds of statements which may just turn out to be attempts to generate hype and pump stocks. Moore's law stopped being true because of physical limitations and that might very well be the case with AI research: is the rate of progress in that field going to decrease at some point and, if so, will it be before we reach the singularity?

Also, does OpenAI truly believe that already introducing AI into the workforce is the only way forward or are they saying that because they want to get ahead of all their competitors when it comes to potentially launching the next industrial revolution? Do they truly believe that collaborating with the (US) military-industrial complex is "for the good of humanity"? How is it not idealistic to think that everyone will see equal benefit from AI with their current approach to introducing it into society? Sure, employees might become more productive, but that results in hiring less workers or replacing them entirely, not an increase in pay or decrease in working hours. How would introducing AI be different to the invention of the loom?

The way I see it, the most likely outcome is that the bourgeoisie will benefit the most from it, unless AGI ends up being benevolent and gets rid of them if and when it takes the world over. The fact of the matter is that the state and the ultra-rich are consistently the first to take control and make use of new technologies so that they can maintain the status quo. There is no reason to think that that is not the case with AI, especially when seeing how much the literal richest men in the world are willing to invest into AI; it's no coincidence that OpenAI was privatised and, if nothing is done, it will only be beholden to the shareholders (specifically the owners of the means of production) rather than the rest of us.
